chapters.title: The Passion of Steve Jobs
chapters.sourcePressure: Steve Jobs and the Stanford advice open Rule 1 by weakening passion-first career folklore without yet replacing it.
chapters.coreMove: Separate an inspiring success story from usable evidence before letting it guide a career decision.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating the point as a dunk on Steve Jobs or as proof that love for work never matters.

chapters.title: Passion Is Rare
chapters.sourcePressure: Roadtrip Nation, Ira Glass, and the Canadian student statistic show messy paths and weak passion-to-work mapping.
chapters.coreMove: Test whether an interest is actually career-ready instead of treating any strong preference as a job map.
chapters.commonMisread: Reducing the point to never trust interests or pretending hobbies have no career signal.

chapters.title: Passion Is Dangerous
chapters.sourcePressure: Passion-first thinking can create stress, burnout, over-monitoring, and premature identity pressure.
chapters.coreMove: Stop using immediate emotional fit as a verdict when early work may still be too immature to judge.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning this into advice to stay in every bad job or ignore exploitation.

chapters.title: The Clarity of the Craftsman
chapters.sourcePressure: The craftsman mindset is the alternative to the passion mindset, supported by Jordan Tice and patient craft development.
chapters.coreMove: Shift attention from whether work serves you to what valuable contribution you can make next.
chapters.commonMisread: Flattening the craftsman mindset into hustle rhetoric or accepting growthless work.

chapters.title: Career Capital
chapters.sourcePressure: Career capital is rare and valuable skill that functions like currency for later control, creativity, and compelling work.
chapters.coreMove: Price desirable work traits as things bought with rare and valuable skill, not requested as entitlements.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating career capital as salary status or moral worth.

chapters.title: The Career Capitalists
chapters.sourcePressure: Career capitalists build rare skill before demanding autonomy, mission, or ideal conditions.
chapters.coreMove: Sequence autonomy, mission, and ideal conditions after compounding skill rather than before it.
chapters.commonMisread: Making patience into passive waiting instead of active compounding.

chapters.title: Becoming a Craftsman
chapters.sourcePressure: The support is procedural: move from craftsman posture to disciplined skill-building, where effort counts only when it improves output.
chapters.coreMove: Turn effort into targeted practice that sharpens output and portable value.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating busyness, long hours, or repetition as becoming a craftsman.

chapters.title: The Dream-Job Elixir
chapters.sourcePressure: Control is the next major reward bought by career capital, and it becomes dangerous when pursued without leverage.
chapters.coreMove: Recognize control as a powerful reward that becomes stable only when backed by career capital.
chapters.commonMisread: Equating control with quitting, remote work, or freedom from obligation.

chapters.title: The First Control Trap
chapters.sourcePressure: The first control trap is stakeholder resistance when valuable people try to convert leverage into more control.
chapters.coreMove: Interpret resistance to your control move as a signal about value at risk, then test whether the move is still sound.
chapters.commonMisread: Assuming all pushback proves you are valuable and therefore right.

chapters.title: The Second Control Trap
chapters.sourcePressure: The second control trap is autonomy pursued without enough durable support beneath it.
chapters.coreMove: Reject control moves whose support is too thin to survive the first hard test.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating this as generic risk-aversion or never leaving unless success is guaranteed.

chapters.title: Avoiding the Control Traps
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter synthesizes the two control traps and asks for practical judgment rather than a formula.
chapters.coreMove: Run a two-trap test that asks both whether you have enough value to face resistance and enough support to survive freedom.
chapters.commonMisread: Inventing a neat yes/no formula or treating one trap as the only danger.

chapters.title: The Meaningful Life of Pardis Sabeti
chapters.sourcePressure: Rule 4 opens through Pardis Sabeti and mission, but support is narrow and forbids unsupported biography.
chapters.coreMove: Turn earned control into the question of what larger mission that freedom can serve.
chapters.commonMisread: Inventing Sabeti biography or treating mission as a return to passion-first searching.

chapters.title: Missions Require Capital
chapters.sourcePressure: Mission connects to earlier skill, leverage, and career capital, and mission talk without prior support stays weak.
chapters.coreMove: Earn mission by building enough capital to see and act near a real frontier.
chapters.commonMisread: Making mission sound like a personal slogan anyone can declare immediately.

chapters.title: Missions Require Little Bets
chapters.sourcePressure: Little bets come after mission capital and before marketing, so the focus is experiments rather than invented case studies.
chapters.coreMove: Use small, disciplined bets to discover which mission direction survives contact with reality.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating little bets as random dabbling or low-stakes procrastination.

chapters.title: Missions Require Marketing
chapters.sourcePressure: Marketing is the final mission ingredient after support and discovery; visibility gives a mission public force.
chapters.coreMove: Give a clarified mission enough visibility that the right people can notice, test, and amplify it.
chapters.commonMisread: Confusing marketing with self-promotion, virality, or empty personal branding.

chapters.title: Conclusion
chapters.sourcePressure: The conclusion synthesizes the four-rule path: reject passion as a starting rule, build rare skill, convert skill into control, and organize work around mission.
chapters.coreMove: Use the full sequence: stop hunting for passion, build capital, trade it for control, and aim it at a supported mission.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning the conclusion into a motivational recap or unsupported new framework.
